question.text: What does safe driving take beyond vehicle basics and rules?

answer.text: Safe driving takes more than vehicle basics and memorized rules; it also needs good judgment, reflexes, experience, patience and common sense.

teaching.text: Knowing the rules is the start; judgment and patience finish the job. Remember: judgment, patience, common sense.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Safe driving takes more than vehicle basics and memorized rules; it also needs good judgment, reflexes, experience, patience and common sense.

question.text: How does a teen driver build skill and confidence?

answer.text: A teen's skill and confidence grow through practice, first on the driver education range, then with a parent, guardian or designated licensed adult twenty-one or older, and later alone once licensed.

teaching.text: Each supervised stage adds experience before a teen drives alone. Remember: range, then adult, then alone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A teen's skill and confidence grow through practice, first on the driver education range, then with a parent, guardian or designated licensed adult twenty-one or older, and later alone once licensed.

question.text: What risk do experienced middle-aged drivers face?

answer.text: Experienced middle-aged drivers can become complacent, and driving on autopilot leaves them less tuned to the risks around them.

teaching.text: Familiar routes can lull experienced drivers into missing risks. Remember: autopilot dulls awareness.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Experienced middle-aged drivers can become complacent, and driving on autopilot leaves them less tuned to the risks around them.

question.text: How can older drivers sharpen their skills?

answer.text: Older drivers can improve through added training, and AAA RoadWise Driver and AARP Driver Safety offer refresher courses, listed at Michigan.gov slash AgingDriver.

teaching.text: No driver is finished learning; refresher courses keep skills sharp. Remember: refresher courses help.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Older drivers can improve through added training, and AAA RoadWise Driver and AARP Driver Safety offer refresher courses, listed at Michigan.gov slash AgingDriver.

question.text: What do aggressive drivers do?

answer.text: Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave, pass illegally on the right, and may gesture, yell, honk or flash their headlights.

teaching.text: Tailgating, weaving and illegal passing on the right are signs of aggression. Remember: speed, tailgate, weave, gesture.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Aggressive drivers run stop signs and red lights, speed, tailgate, weave, pass illegally on the right, and may gesture, yell, honk or flash their headlights.

question.text: What can happen if you answer aggression in kind?

answer.text: Answering aggression in kind can escalate into road rage, where a weapon or the vehicle itself is used to attack another driver.

teaching.text: Answering anger with anger can turn a bad moment into road rage. Remember: anger escalates to rage.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Answering aggression in kind can escalate into road rage, where a weapon or the vehicle itself is used to attack another driver.

question.text: What share of traffic deaths have officials linked to aggressive driving?

answer.text: Federal highway safety officials have estimated that aggressive driving behaviors cause sixty-six percent of all traffic fatalities.

teaching.text: Officials have estimated aggressive driving causes sixty-six percent of traffic deaths. Remember: aggression kills most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Federal highway safety officials have estimated that aggressive driving behaviors cause sixty-six percent of all traffic fatalities.

question.text: What should you do when another driver merges or turns badly?

answer.text: Merge smoothly, and when another driver merges or turns badly, slow down, give room, and back off rather than trying to prove you are right.

teaching.text: Let a bad merge go, instead of trying to prove a point. Remember: back off, don't prove it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Merge smoothly, and when another driver merges or turns badly, slow down, give room, and back off rather than trying to prove you are right.

question.text: Someone tailgates you while you pass in the left lane. What should you do?

answer.text: If someone tailgates you while you pass in the left lane, move back right when safe and let faster traffic go, since a backed-up left lane tempts aggressive drivers to take risks.

teaching.text: After passing, return to the right so faster traffic can go. Remember: pass, then move right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If someone tailgates you while you pass in the left lane, move back right when safe and let faster traffic go, since a backed-up left lane tempts aggressive drivers to take risks.

question.text: Another driver tailgates you. How do you handle it?

answer.text: If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass so the unsafe driver is ahead where you can see them.

teaching.text: A tailgater ahead of you is a danger you can see. Remember: let tailgaters go ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If another driver tailgates you, pull over and let them pass so the unsafe driver is ahead where you can see them.

question.text: How should you handle gestures on the road?

answer.text: Never gesture at other drivers in anger, and if you made a mistake and someone gestures, signal that you are sorry.

teaching.text: An apology signal can end a tense moment. Remember: never gesture; apologize.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never gesture at other drivers in anger, and if you made a mistake and someone gestures, signal that you are sorry.

question.text: What should you do when confronted by an aggressive driver?

answer.text: When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore gestures or insults, and call police to report them when safe.

teaching.text: Looking away and moving away keeps a confrontation from growing. Remember: get away, no eye contact.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When confronted by an aggressive driver, get out of the way, avoid eye contact, ignore gestures or insults, and call police to report them when safe.

question.text: What should you do if an aggressive driver crashes ahead?

answer.text: If an aggressive driver crashes farther ahead, stop a safe distance from the scene, wait for police and report what you saw.

teaching.text: Be a calm witness from a safe distance, and let police handle it. Remember: stop back, report it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an aggressive driver crashes farther ahead, stop a safe distance from the scene, wait for police and report what you saw.

question.text: Where on the road do crashes cause the most deaths and serious injuries?

answer.text: Intersection crashes cause more traffic deaths and serious injuries than crashes on any other part of the road.

teaching.text: More deaths and serious injuries happen at intersections than anywhere else. Remember: intersections are deadliest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Intersection crashes cause more traffic deaths and serious injuries than crashes on any other part of the road.

question.text: What should you check as you approach an intersection?

answer.text: Approaching an intersection, check oncoming and cross traffic, pedestrians, signals, signs, markings, road condition and blind areas, and let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do.

teaching.text: If you cannot tell what another driver will do, let them go first. Remember: check everything, yield if unsure.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Approaching an intersection, check oncoming and cross traffic, pedestrians, signals, signs, markings, road condition and blind areas, and let others go first whenever you are unsure what they will do.

question.text: Why look twice for motorcycles and bicycles at intersections?

answer.text: Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds at intersections because their speed and distance are hard to judge.

teaching.text: A quick glance can miss a small rider, so look again. Remember: look twice for riders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds at intersections because their speed and distance are hard to judge.

question.text: What should you do when your view at an intersection is blocked?

answer.text: When trees, buildings or snow piles block your view at an intersection, creep forward slowly until you can see past them.

teaching.text: Stop first, then edge forward until you can see past what blocks your view. Remember: creep until you see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When trees, buildings or snow piles block your view at an intersection, creep forward slowly until you can see past them.

question.text: What is a freeway, and who is banned from it?

answer.text: Freeways carry one-direction traffic with no stops or intersections, and pedestrians, motorcycles of one hundred twenty-four cubic centimeters or less, mopeds, bicycles, ATVs and slow-moving vehicles are banned from them.

teaching.text: Everything on a freeway is meant to move at freeway speed. Remember: no stops, no slow users.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Freeways carry one-direction traffic with no stops or intersections, and pedestrians, motorcycles of one hundred twenty-four cubic centimeters or less, mopeds, bicycles, ATVs and slow-moving vehicles are banned from them.

question.text: Why watch for Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs near ramps?

answer.text: Entrance ramps often sit beside exit ramps, so watch for Do Not Enter, Wrong Way and speed limit signs.

teaching.text: Make sure you are on the entrance ramp before you speed up. Remember: entrances sit beside exits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Entrance ramps often sit beside exit ramps, so watch for Do Not Enter, Wrong Way and speed limit signs.

question.text: How do you use an acceleration lane to merge?

answer.text: Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed, signal, check mirrors and glance over your shoulder, then merge into a safe gap, yielding to freeway traffic and not counting on others to let you in.

teaching.text: Reach freeway speed, look, then merge into a gap you chose. Remember: speed up, signal, look, merge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed, signal, check mirrors and glance over your shoulder, then merge into a safe gap, yielding to freeway traffic and not counting on others to let you in.

question.text: What do merge signs near entrances ask of freeway drivers?

answer.text: Merge signs near entrances warn of entering traffic; adjust speed or change lanes safely to help them merge, and watch for drivers who brake or swerve suddenly toward an exit.

teaching.text: Freeway drivers help entering traffic by adjusting speed or moving over. Remember: help merging traffic in.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Merge signs near entrances warn of entering traffic; adjust speed or change lanes safely to help them merge, and watch for drivers who brake or swerve suddenly toward an exit.

question.text: Under Michigan's merge law, who must yield and adjust?

answer.text: Michigan's merge law, MCL two hundred fifty-seven point six four nine(seven), means the merging driver must yield to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard and adjust speed and position to merge safely, whether entering or leaving the freeway.

teaching.text: The merging driver carries the duty to yield and adjust. Remember: merging driver yields.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Michigan's merge law, MCL two hundred fifty-seven point six four nine(seven), means the merging driver must yield to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard and adjust speed and position to merge safely, whether entering or leaving the freeway.

question.text: When merging onto a freeway, who adjusts speed and position?

answer.text: The merging driver, not freeway traffic, must adjust speed and placement to merge safely.

teaching.text: Freeway traffic does not have to make room for you. Remember: the merger adjusts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The merging driver, not freeway traffic, must adjust speed and placement to merge safely.

question.text: On a two-lane freeway, when may you leave the right lane?

answer.text: On a two-lane freeway keep right except to pass, exit left, let a vehicle merge, in heavy congestion, or when emergency vehicles or construction workers are on the shoulders.

teaching.text: The right lane is home on a two-lane freeway. Remember: keep right with exceptions.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a two-lane freeway keep right except to pass, exit left, let a vehicle merge, in heavy congestion, or when emergency vehicles or construction workers are on the shoulders.

question.text: With three or more lanes your way, which lane may you use?

answer.text: With three or more lanes in your direction you may use any lane, but stay with the slower traffic if driving at or near the minimum speed.

teaching.text: On wide freeways, slow drivers stay with the slower traffic. Remember: any lane, slow keeps right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With three or more lanes in your direction you may use any lane, but stay with the slower traffic if driving at or near the minimum speed.

question.text: Who may use an HOV lane, and when?

answer.text: HOV lanes require two or more occupants during peak hours such as rush hour, are open to everyone outside those hours, and motorcycles may use them any time.

teaching.text: The HOV limit applies only at peak hours, and motorcycles may always use it. Remember: two aboard at peak hours.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: HOV lanes require two or more occupants during peak hours such as rush hour, are open to everyone outside those hours, and motorcycles may use them any time.

question.text: When and how may you stop on a freeway?

answer.text: Stop on a freeway only in an emergency, and then use hazard flashers, slow gradually and pull completely off the pavement.

teaching.text: A stopped car belongs fully off the pavement with flashers on. Remember: emergencies only, fully off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stop on a freeway only in an emergency, and then use hazard flashers, slow gradually and pull completely off the pavement.

question.text: How do you exit a freeway safely?

answer.text: To exit, check traffic and signal into the deceleration lane, and do not slow down until you are fully in that lane, then obey the ramp speed limit since many ramps curve sharply.

teaching.text: Hold your speed until you are in the deceleration lane, then slow for the ramp. Remember: slow only in decel lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To exit, check traffic and signal into the deceleration lane, and do not slow down until you are fully in that lane, then obey the ramp speed limit since many ramps curve sharply.

question.text: What do you do if you miss your freeway exit?

answer.text: If you miss your exit, never back up, turn around or use the median crossover, which is only for emergency and MDOT vehicles; go to the next exit and come back.

teaching.text: The crossover is for emergency and MDOT vehicles only. Remember: missed exit, take the next.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you miss your exit, never back up, turn around or use the median crossover, which is only for emergency and MDOT vehicles; go to the next exit and come back.

question.text: How does lane choice differ between two-lane and wider freeways?

answer.text: On a two-lane freeway you keep right except in listed cases, but with three or more lanes any lane is allowed unless you are near the minimum speed.

teaching.text: Two lanes means keep right; three or more means choose, unless you are slow. Remember: two lanes keep right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a two-lane freeway you keep right except in listed cases, but with three or more lanes any lane is allowed unless you are near the minimum speed.

question.text: When do HOV rules apply, and who is always exempt?

answer.text: HOV restrictions apply only during peak hours, and motorcycles are exempt at all times.

teaching.text: Peak hours only, and motorcycles always. Remember: peak hours; motorcycles exempt.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: HOV restrictions apply only during peak hours, and motorcycles are exempt at all times.

question.text: Why is fatigue such a danger on freeways?

answer.text: Fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers, since the steady hum of wind, tires and engine can make you sleepy or hypnotized.

teaching.text: The steady freeway hum can lull you to sleep. Remember: the hum makes you sleepy.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Fatigue is one of the biggest freeway dangers, since the steady hum of wind, tires and engine can make you sleepy or hypnotized.

question.text: What should you do when you feel tired on a long drive?

answer.text: Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs; if tired, take a ten-minute break at least every two hours or let someone else drive.

teaching.text: A short break every two hours does what coffee cannot. Remember: breaks beat coffee.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not rely on coffee or stay-awake drugs; if tired, take a ten-minute break at least every two hours or let someone else drive.

question.text: If you must keep driving tired, how do you stay alert?

answer.text: If you must keep driving while tired, keep moving your eyes across the road, check mirrors, and look near, far, left and right.

teaching.text: Moving your eyes keeps your mind on the road. Remember: keep your eyes moving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you must keep driving while tired, keep moving your eyes across the road, check mirrors, and look near, far, left and right.

question.text: Where does cruise control work best, and at what setting?

answer.text: Cruise control works best in rural areas with light traffic; set it at or below the speed limit.

teaching.text: Light rural traffic is where cruise control fits. Remember: rural, light traffic, at limit.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cruise control works best in rural areas with light traffic; set it at or below the speed limit.

question.text: What cancels cruise control: the accelerator or the brake?

answer.text: Pressing the accelerator does not cancel cruise control, but pressing the brake pedal does.

teaching.text: Only the brake turns cruise control off. Remember: brake cancels, gas doesn't.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pressing the accelerator does not cancel cruise control, but pressing the brake pedal does.

question.text: When should you avoid cruise control?

answer.text: Avoid cruise control in heavy traffic, near many ramps, on roads slick with rain, snow or ice, and when towing heavy loads, since constant resetting distracts you.

teaching.text: Heavy traffic, ramps, slick roads and towing all call for full control. Remember: no cruise in heavy traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid cruise control in heavy traffic, near many ramps, on roads slick with rain, snow or ice, and when towing heavy loads, since constant resetting distracts you.

question.text: What happens to cruise control when you tap the accelerator or the brake?

answer.text: Tapping the accelerator leaves cruise control on, but touching the brake turns it off.

teaching.text: The gas pedal leaves cruise on; the brake ends it. Remember: gas keeps it, brake ends it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tapping the accelerator leaves cruise control on, but touching the brake turns it off.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: gas keeps it, brake ends it

question.text: An oncoming vehicle is in your lane. What do you do?

answer.text: If an oncoming vehicle is in your lane, tap the horn if there is time, brake hard without locking the wheels if you lack anti-lock brakes, and look for an escape route on the right edge.

teaching.text: Your escape route is to the right, never across into the left lane. Remember: horn, brake, escape right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an oncoming vehicle is in your lane, tap the horn if there is time, brake hard without locking the wheels if you lack anti-lock brakes, and look for an escape route on the right edge.

question.text: Why avoid swerving left from an oncoming vehicle?

answer.text: Avoid swerving left from an oncoming vehicle, because its driver may notice you and return to the proper lane; stop in your lane only if there is room and you cannot pull off.

teaching.text: The other driver may return to their lane, right where you swerved. Remember: never swerve left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid swerving left from an oncoming vehicle, because its driver may notice you and return to the proper lane; stop in your lane only if there is room and you cannot pull off.

question.text: You cannot stop before hitting a vehicle. What then?

answer.text: If you cannot stop before hitting another vehicle, steer around it, turning no more than you need.

teaching.text: Steer around, using only as much turn as you need. Remember: steer around, just enough.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you cannot stop before hitting another vehicle, steer around it, turning no more than you need.

question.text: What causes most skids?

answer.text: Most skids come from turning too fast or stopping suddenly on slippery pavement, so test the brakes lightly to feel the road.

teaching.text: Too fast in a turn or too sudden a stop starts most skids. Remember: too fast, too sudden.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most skids come from turning too fast or stopping suddenly on slippery pavement, so test the brakes lightly to feel the road.

question.text: How do you steer out of a skid?

answer.text: In a skid, lift off the accelerator, point the front wheels only where you want to go, expect a secondary skid the other way, steer again, then straighten the wheels.

teaching.text: Look and steer where you want to go, and expect a second slide. Remember: look and steer where going.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a skid, lift off the accelerator, point the front wheels only where you want to go, expect a secondary skid the other way, steer again, then straighten the wheels.

question.text: How do anti-lock braking and threshold braking differ?

answer.text: Anti-lock brakes need hard, firm pressure from the start held until you stop, and vibration or pulsing is normal, while without anti-lock you brake just short of locking and release and reapply if the wheels lock, called threshold or controlled braking.

teaching.text: Anti-lock means hold the pressure; standard means brake just short of locking. Remember: anti-lock hold; threshold release.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Anti-lock brakes need hard, firm pressure from the start held until you stop, and vibration or pulsing is normal, while without anti-lock you brake just short of locking and release and reapply if the wheels lock, called threshold or controlled braking.

question.text: How do you slow and stop in normal conditions?

answer.text: Under normal conditions, a steady, firm push on the brake pedal is how you slow and stop.

teaching.text: Everyday stops use a steady, firm push. Remember: steady, firm brake push.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under normal conditions, a steady, firm push on the brake pedal is how you slow and stop.

question.text: How do you brake hard with standard brakes versus anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: With standard brakes, steady pressure without locking the wheels keeps them turning so you can steer, while with full anti-lock brakes you keep pressing and steer.

teaching.text: Turning wheels can still steer, so do not lock them. Remember: standard: don't lock; anti-lock: press.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With standard brakes, steady pressure without locking the wheels keeps them turning so you can steer, while with full anti-lock brakes you keep pressing and steer.

question.text: What is the best way to prepare a car for winter travel?

answer.text: Pre-winter maintenance is the best way to travel safely: check power steering, brake, washer and oil fluids, keep antifreeze strong and fresh, and consider washer fluid with antifreeze.

teaching.text: Get your fluids and antifreeze ready before winter arrives. Remember: maintain before winter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pre-winter maintenance is the best way to travel safely: check power steering, brake, washer and oil fluids, keep antifreeze strong and fresh, and consider washer fluid with antifreeze.

question.text: How should you drive in fog, rain or snow?

answer.text: In fog, rain or snow leave extra time, drive slower and increase following distance, and remember bridges and underpasses freeze before the road in cold weather.

teaching.text: Slow down and leave more room, and expect bridges to freeze first. Remember: slower, longer gaps, icy bridges.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In fog, rain or snow leave extra time, drive slower and increase following distance, and remember bridges and underpasses freeze before the road in cold weather.

question.text: When is a wet road slickest, and what gap should you keep?

answer.text: Roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain because oil from vehicles has not yet washed off, so slow down, take extra care at intersections, and allow at least twice the normal following distance.

teaching.text: Oil makes the first rain slickest, so double your gap. Remember: first half hour, double gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Roads are slickest in the first half hour of rain because oil from vehicles has not yet washed off, so slow down, take extra care at intersections, and allow at least twice the normal following distance.

question.text: What should you do after driving through deep water?

answer.text: After deep water or heavy rain, test your brakes, which may pull or fail to hold, and press gently while driving slowly until they work normally.

teaching.text: Wet brakes may pull or fail; press gently until they work. Remember: test wet brakes gently.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After deep water or heavy rain, test your brakes, which may pull or fail to hold, and press gently while driving slowly until they work normally.

question.text: What is hydroplaning, and what makes it more likely?

answer.text: Hydroplaning happens when tires ride on top of water and can cost you control; worn tires, low pressure and too much speed make it more likely.

teaching.text: Good tires, proper pressure and lower speed fight hydroplaning. Remember: tires surf on water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning happens when tires ride on top of water and can cost you control; worn tires, low pressure and too much speed make it more likely.

question.text: May you drive around barricades on a flooded road?

answer.text: Never drive around barricades closing a flooded road, since debris, power lines or a washed-out road may be hidden; without barricades, consider another route, and deep water can damage the engine.

teaching.text: The water may hide debris, power lines or a missing road. Remember: never pass flood barricades.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive around barricades closing a flooded road, since debris, power lines or a washed-out road may be hidden; without barricades, consider another route, and deep water can damage the engine.

question.text: How should you drive in fog, and what if you cannot see?

answer.text: Drive slowly in fog with low-beam headlights, ready to stop, and if you cannot see at all, pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait.

teaching.text: Low beams and slow speed in fog; pull off if you cannot see. Remember: low beams, pull off if blind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drive slowly in fog with low-beam headlights, ready to stop, and if you cannot see at all, pull off, turn on the four-way flashers and wait.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: low beams, pull off if blind

question.text: How should you drive on ice and snow?

answer.text: On ice and snow drive slowly, slow down gradually, and listen and watch for snowmobiles and trail crossing signs, since stopping power is reduced.

teaching.text: Stopping power drops on ice, so make every move gentle. Remember: slow and gradual on ice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On ice and snow drive slowly, slow down gradually, and listen and watch for snowmobiles and trail crossing signs, since stopping power is reduced.
